why are tertiary carbocations more stable than primary ones?
Tertiary carbocations are more stable for two main reasons:
1. Hyperconjugation: neighbouring C–H and C–C bonds donate electron density into the empty p orbital.
2. Inductive effect: alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon.
More alkyl groups means more stabilisation, so tertiary > secondary > primary.

I don't get hyperconjugation, explain it more simply with an example
Think of the empty p orbital as a gap that nearby bonds can partly fill.
Example: in the tert-butyl cation, nine C–H bonds sit next to the positive carbon and each shares a little electron density.
Sharing the charge over more bonds lowers the energy, which is what 'more stable' means.
